title: Common Summations Table
summary: Simple, double summations and frequent patterns used in algorithm analysis. It includes closed formulas, asymptotic order, context of appearance in code and useful properties for transforming sums.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a simple, nested, or logarithmic loop generates a sum.
Use closed formulas for simple summations of constants, powers, geometric, logarithmic and harmonic formulas.
Solve double sums inside out, first converting the inner sum into closed form.
Distinguish double summations with fixed limits, variable limits and logarithmic inner loops.
Apply linearity, index change, telescoping, separation of terms and order inversion to simplify summations.
Relate each formula to the type of code structure where it appears.
Use summations as a base mathematical tool for the iteration method and the recursion tree.

terms.label: Summation
terms.definition: Mathematical notation used to represent the cumulative sum of indexed terms.

terms.label: Simple summation
terms.definition: Summation with a single index. Typically appears in simple loops.

terms.label: Double sum
terms.definition: Summation with two nested indices. Appears in nested loops.

terms.label: Triple sum
terms.definition: Summation with three nested indices. It appears in three-loop structures, such as matrix multiplication or tensor traversals.

terms.label: closed form
terms.definition: Expression equivalent to a sum, but without the addition symbol.

terms.label: geometric series
terms.definition: Sum whose terms have the form r^i.

terms.label: Telescopic
terms.definition: Summation where consecutive terms cancel, leaving only the extremes.

learningObjectives.text: Understand why summations constantly appear when counting code block executions.
Distinguish simple, double and triple additions.

content.text: In algorithm analysis, summations constantly appear when counting how many times a block of code is executed. Knowing how to solve them—or at least recognize them—is as important as knowing how to calculate limits.

This section brings together the most common summations organized into three levels of complexity: simple (a single index), double (two nested indices) and triple (three nested indices). For each one, the addition notation, its closed form and an example of what type of code it appears in are shown.
